column1: Physics|What is the SI unit of force?|Newton|Joule|Watt|Pascal|Force is measured in newtons; a newton is equivalent to kg·m/s².
Physics|What is the SI unit of energy?|Joule|Newton|Watt|Ampere|A joule measures energy or work. A watt measures the rate of energy transfer.
Physics|What is the SI unit of power?|Watt|Joule|Metre|Coulomb|Power is energy transferred per unit time; one watt equals one joule per second.

Physics|What does speed measure?|Distance travelled per unit time|Change in temperature per unit time|Mass per unit volume|Force per unit area|Speed is distance divided by elapsed time. Velocity also includes direction.

Physics|What does acceleration measure?|Change in velocity per unit time|Only total distance|Only total mass|Only total energy|Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and can result from changing speed or direction.

Physics|What is inertia?|Resistance to a change in state of motion|Energy produced by a battery|The total charge on a proton|The speed of a wave|Inertia describes the tendency to retain rest or uniform motion unless a net external force acts.

Physics|What is the approximate value of gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface?|9.8 m/s²|98 m/s²|0.98 m/s²|980 m/s²|Near the surface, gravitational acceleration is approximately 9.8 m/s²; it varies slightly with location.
Physics|Which quantity is a vector?|Force|Mass|Time|Temperature|A vector has magnitude and direction. Force and displacement are examples.
Physics|Which quantity is scalar?|Mass|Displacement|Velocity|Acceleration|Mass has magnitude but no direction; the other listed quantities are vectors.
Physics|What does pressure equal?|Force divided by area|Area divided by force|Mass multiplied by speed|Energy multiplied by time|Pressure is normal force per unit area, measured in pascals in SI.

Physics|Which relation states Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature?|V = IR|V = I/R|V = R/I|V = I + R|Potential difference equals current times resistance under the conditions in which Ohm's law applies.
Physics|Which instrument measures electric current?|Ammeter|Voltmeter|Barometer|Thermometer|An ammeter measures current and is ordinarily connected in series with the branch being measured.
Physics|Which instrument measures potential difference?|Voltmeter|Ammeter|Hydrometer|Anemometer|A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points and is connected across them.

Physics|Which arrangement gives appliances the same supply voltage in a typical household circuit?|Parallel connection|Series connection|One open circuit for all appliances|A circuit without a return path|In parallel branches, appliances have the same potential difference and can operate independently.

Physics|Which mirror is commonly used as a vehicle rear-view mirror for a wider field of view?|Convex mirror|Concave mirror|Plane mirror only in every case|A cylindrical lens|A convex mirror gives an erect diminished image and a wider field of view.
Physics|Which lens can converge parallel light rays?|Convex lens|Concave lens|Opaque plate|Plane mirror|A convex lens can converge parallel rays to a focus under ordinary conditions.

Physics|Why can sound not travel through an ideal vacuum?|It requires a material medium|It needs sunlight|It travels only through metals|Its frequency becomes infinite|Sound is a mechanical wave and requires particles of a medium to carry the disturbance.
Physics|What is the unit of frequency?|Hertz|Volt|Ohm|Kelvin|One hertz means one cycle per second.

Chemistry|Which subatomic particle has a negative electric charge?|Electron|Proton|Neutron|Atomic nucleus as a whole|Electrons carry negative charge; protons are positive and neutrons have no net charge.

Chemistry|What does the atomic number represent?|Number of protons in the nucleus|Number of neutrons only|Mass in kilograms|Number of chemical bonds in every compound|The atomic number identifies an element by its proton count.

Chemistry|What are isotopes?|Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts|Atoms with identical protons and neutrons but different names|Only charged molecules|Compounds with identical formulas|Isotopes share atomic number but differ in neutron count and therefore mass number.
Chemistry|Which pH value indicates an acidic aqueous solution at ordinary conditions?|3|7|9|12|A pH below 7 is acidic at ordinary classroom conditions; pH 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.

Chemistry|What are the usual products of acid-base neutralization?|Salt and water|Only oxygen|Only hydrogen|Only carbon dioxide|An acid and a base commonly react to form a salt and water; specific chemistry depends on the reactants.
Chemistry|What is the chemical formula of common salt?|NaCl|NaOH|HCl|CaCO3|Common salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.
Chemistry|What is the chemical formula of water?|H2O|CO2|O2|H2O2|A water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
Chemistry|Which gas is commonly released when an acid reacts with a carbonate?|Carbon dioxide|Nitrogen|Oxygen|Argon|Acids react with carbonates to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

Chemistry|What is rusting mainly an example of?|Oxidation of iron in the presence of moisture and oxygen|Melting of iron without chemical change|Freezing of water|Evaporation of salt|Rusting is a chemical change involving iron, oxygen and water.

Chemistry|Which process separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?|Filtration|Distillation only|Sublimation only|Electrolysis only|A filter retains insoluble particles while the liquid passes through.

Chemistry|Which process can separate water from a salt solution and collect the water?|Distillation|Simple filtration|Magnetic separation|Sieving|Distillation vaporizes water and condenses it separately; ordinary filtration does not remove dissolved salt.

Chemistry|What is a catalyst?|A substance that changes reaction rate without being consumed overall|A reactant always used up completely|Any final product|A substance that always stops every reaction|A catalyst participates in intermediate steps but is regenerated overall and changes the reaction pathway.
Chemistry|Which is a physical change?|Melting ice|Burning paper|Rusting iron|Cooking an egg|Melting changes state without changing water's chemical identity.
Chemistry|Which is a chemical change?|Burning magnesium|Cutting paper|Freezing water|Breaking glass|Burning magnesium forms a new substance, magnesium oxide; the others are physical changes.
Biology|What is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms?|Cell|Atom only|Tissue only|Organ only|Cells are the basic units of life; tissues and organs are built from cells.

Biology|Which cell structure controls most activities and contains chromosomes in a typical eukaryotic cell?|Nucleus|Cell wall|Vacuole only|Cell membrane only|The nucleus contains most genetic material and contributes to regulation of cellular activities.

Biology|Which organelle is especially associated with aerobic cellular respiration?|Mitochondrion|Ribosome|Golgi apparatus|Chloroplast only|Mitochondria perform major stages of aerobic respiration and ATP production.
Biology|Which pigment helps capture light energy for photosynthesis?|Chlorophyll|Haemoglobin|Melanin|Keratin|Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light used in photosynthesis.

Biology|Which plant tissue mainly transports water and mineral ions from roots?|Xylem|Phloem|Epidermis only|Pollen|Xylem conducts water and mineral ions; phloem transports sugars and other organic solutes.
Biology|Which plant tissue mainly transports sugars from sources to sinks?|Phloem|Xylem|Root hair only|Stomata only|Phloem moves photosynthetic products toward parts that use or store them.
Biology|Which gas is released during oxygenic photosynthesis?|Oxygen|Nitrogen|Methane|Hydrogen|Oxygen is released from the splitting of water during oxygenic photosynthesis.

Biology|Where does most absorption of digested nutrients occur in humans?|Small intestine|Oesophagus|Mouth only|Large intestine only|The small intestine has a large absorptive surface formed by folds, villi and microvilli.
Biology|What is the principal role of red blood cells?|Transporting oxygen|Producing bile|Digesting starch|Forming bone|Haemoglobin in red blood cells binds oxygen and supports its transport.
Biology|Which blood components help with clotting?|Platelets|Red blood cells only|Bile salts|Digestive enzymes|Platelets contribute to forming a clot together with plasma clotting factors.
Biology|Which organs filter blood and form urine?|Kidneys|Lungs|Pancreas|Spleen only|Kidneys filter plasma and adjust water and solute balance while forming urine.

Biology|Which hormone helps lower elevated blood glucose?|Insulin|Adrenaline only|Thyroxine only|Melatonin only|Insulin promotes cellular uptake and storage of glucose; this is a basic biology concept, not personal treatment advice.

Biology|Which nutrient is a major structural material for growth and tissue repair?|Protein|Water only|Salt only|Dietary fibre only|Proteins provide amino acids used to build and maintain tissues; a balanced diet supplies several nutrient groups.

Biology|Which disease is classically associated with severe vitamin C deficiency?|Scurvy|Rickets|Night blindness|Beriberi|Scurvy is associated with vitamin C deficiency; other deficiencies cause different conditions.

Biology|Which vitamin deficiency is classically associated with rickets in children?|Vitamin D|Vitamin C|Vitamin B1|Vitamin K|Vitamin D contributes to calcium regulation and bone mineralization; severe deficiency can lead to rickets.

Biology|What is pollination?|Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma|Formation of soil from rock|Growth of a root hair|Movement of water through xylem|Pollination precedes fertilization in flowering plants and can occur through biotic or abiotic agents.

Biology|What is an ecosystem?|Organisms interacting with one another and their physical environment|Only a list of animals|Only a weather forecast|Only the top layer of soil|An ecosystem includes biotic components and abiotic conditions together with their interactions.

Biology|Which organism is a producer in a typical terrestrial food chain?|Green plant|Tiger|Mushroom|Vulture|Green plants capture energy through photosynthesis; consumers and decomposers have different ecological roles.
Physics|A runner covers 120 metres in 20 seconds at uniform speed. What is the speed?|6 m/s|2400 m/s|100 m/s|0.167 m/s|Divide distance by time: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 metres per second.

Physics|A car's velocity changes from 5 m/s to 17 m/s in 4 seconds. What is its average acceleration?|3 m/s²|12 m/s²|5.5 m/s²|48 m/s²|Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by time: (17 − 5) ÷ 4 = 3 m/s².
Physics|A 2 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s². What net force acts on it?|6 N|1.5 N|5 N|0.67 N|Newton's second law gives net force = mass × acceleration = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

Physics|An object moves at constant velocity in a straight line. What is the net force on it?|Zero|Always equal to its weight|Always increasing|Equal to its mass numerically|Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the vector sum of forces is zero; individual forces may still act.

Physics|A person completes one lap and returns to the starting point. What is their displacement?|Zero|Equal to the lap length|Half the lap length|Necessarily negative|Displacement depends on final minus initial position. The distance travelled is nonzero but displacement is zero.

Physics|What does the slope of a distance-time graph represent during uniform straight-line motion?|Speed|Mass|Force|Pressure|The graph slope is the change in distance divided by the change in time, which is speed.

Physics|What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?|Signed displacement|Instantaneous mass|Pressure|Electric charge|Velocity integrated over time gives displacement; regions below the time axis contribute negatively.
Physics|A 5 N force moves an object 4 metres along the force direction. What work is done?|20 J|1.25 J|9 J|0 J|For force parallel to displacement, work = force × displacement = 5 × 4 = 20 J.
Physics|A 3 kg object travels at 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?|24 J|12 J|48 J|6 J|Kinetic energy is one half of mass times speed squared: 0.5 × 3 × 16 = 24 J.
Physics|Using g = 10 m/s², what gravitational potential energy does a 2 kg object gain when raised 3 metres?|60 J|6 J|15 J|20 J|The gain near Earth's surface is mgh = 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 J.
Physics|A machine transfers 600 joules in 30 seconds. What is its average power?|20 W|18000 W|570 W|0.05 W|Average power is energy divided by time: 600 ÷ 30 = 20 watts.
Physics|A 20 N force acts normally on an area of 0.5 m². What is the pressure?|40 Pa|10 Pa|20.5 Pa|0.025 Pa|Pressure = force ÷ area = 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40 pascals.
Physics|An object has mass 200 g and volume 100 cm³. What is its density?|2 g/cm³|20000 g/cm³|0.5 g/cm³|300 g/cm³|Density is mass per unit volume: 200 ÷ 100 = 2 grams per cubic centimetre.

Physics|Why does a sharp blade cut more readily than a blunt blade under the same normal force?|Its smaller contact area produces greater pressure|It eliminates all friction|Its force must be zero|It changes the material's mass|With equal force, reducing the contact area increases pressure at the edge.

Physics|What mainly explains an object's apparent loss of weight when immersed in a fluid?|An upward buoyant force|Disappearance of its mass|Elimination of gravity|Conversion of all matter to heat|The fluid exerts an upward buoyant force; apparent weight is reduced while the object's mass remains.

Physics|Archimedes' principle relates buoyant force to which quantity?|Weight of displaced fluid|Mass of the object alone|Temperature of the object alone|Volume of air above the fluid only|Buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced by the immersed portion of the object.

Physics|Which mode of heat transfer can operate across empty space?|Radiation|Conduction through particles only|Convection of liquid only|Diffusion of dissolved salt|Thermal radiation is electromagnetic and can propagate through a vacuum.

Physics|Warm water rising within a heated vessel illustrates which heat-transfer mechanism?|Convection|Reflection|Electrical induction|Sublimation|Convection transfers heat through bulk fluid movement, influenced by density differences.

Physics|Heat travelling along a metal rod mainly demonstrates which process?|Conduction|Convection of the solid as a whole|Condensation|Refraction|Conduction transfers energy through interactions within a material without bulk transport of the rod.

Physics|At a fixed pressure, why can temperature remain constant while pure ice melts?|Energy is used for the phase change|No energy enters the ice|Water loses all internal energy|The thermometer creates cold|During melting, supplied energy changes the phase rather than increasing temperature until the transition is complete.

Physics|What is the angle of reflection when the angle of incidence to the normal is 35 degrees?|35 degrees|55 degrees|70 degrees|0 degrees|The law of reflection states that incidence and reflection angles, measured from the normal, are equal.

Physics|Why does a pencil partly submerged in water appear bent?|Light refracts at the water-air boundary|The pencil necessarily breaks|Water emits the image independently|Light can only move in circles|Light changes direction when passing obliquely between media with different refractive indices.

Physics|A plane mirror forms which kind of image of an ordinary object in front of it?|Virtual, erect and the same size|Real, inverted and always larger|Virtual and always half size|Real and always behind the object|A plane mirror image is virtual and erect, with image distance behind the mirror equal to object distance in front.

Physics|Which property of a sound wave mainly determines perceived pitch?|Frequency|The source's mass only|The colour of the medium|Atmospheric pressure alone|Higher frequency generally corresponds to higher pitch; loudness is primarily associated with intensity.
Physics|In a medium, a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 2 m. What is its speed?|100 m/s|25 m/s|52 m/s|0.04 m/s|Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: 50 × 2 = 100 m/s.
Physics|A current of 2 A flows for 5 seconds. How much charge passes a point?|10 C|2.5 C|7 C|0.4 C|Charge = current × time = 2 × 5 = 10 coulombs.
Physics|A 6 V potential difference is applied across a 3 ohm ohmic resistor. What is the current?|2 A|18 A|9 A|0.5 A|Ohm's law gives current = voltage ÷ resistance = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A.
Physics|What is the total resistance of 2 ohm and 4 ohm resistors connected in series?|6 ohms|1.33 ohms|8 ohms|2 ohms|Series resistances add because the same current flows through each resistor.

Physics|Two identical 6 ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is their equivalent resistance?|3 ohms|12 ohms|36 ohms|6 ohms|For two equal parallel resistors, equivalent resistance is half of either resistance; reciprocal conductances add.
Physics|A device draws 2 A from a 12 V supply. What electrical power does it use?|24 W|6 W|14 W|0.167 W|Electrical power = voltage × current = 12 × 2 = 24 watts.

Physics|Why is a fuse placed in a circuit?|To interrupt excessive current by melting its element|To guarantee zero resistance in every appliance|To increase the supply voltage indefinitely|To store electrical charge permanently|A correctly rated fuse opens the circuit if current exceeds the level its element can safely carry.

Physics|Which observation shows that an electric current can have a magnetic effect?|A compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire|A dry stone becomes lighter in sunlight|Water freezes in a refrigerator|A mirror reflects a face|A current produces a magnetic field around its conductor, which can affect a nearby compass.
Chemistry|What is the mass number of an atom with 6 protons and 7 neutrons?|13|6|7|42|Mass number counts nucleons: protons plus neutrons, so 6 + 7 = 13.
Chemistry|A neutral atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does it have?|11|10|12|22|Electrical neutrality requires equal numbers of protons and electrons.

Chemistry|An atom loses one electron without changing its nucleus. What does it become?|A positively charged ion|A new element automatically|A negatively charged ion|A neutron|Losing a negative charge leaves a net positive charge; the element's proton count stays unchanged.

Chemistry|What happens when a neutral atom gains an electron?|It becomes a negative ion|Its atomic number increases by one|It loses every proton|It becomes electrically neutral by definition|An added electron makes electron count exceed proton count, giving a net negative charge.

Chemistry|Why must a chemical equation be balanced?|Atoms of each element are conserved in an ordinary chemical reaction|Reactant names must have equal word lengths|All products must be gases|Every reaction has exactly two reactants|Balancing coefficients accounts for the same number of each type of atom before and after the reaction.

Chemistry|Which balanced equation describes hydrogen reacting with oxygen to form water?|2H2 + O2 → 2H2O|H2 + O2 → H2O|H2 + 2O2 → H2O|2H2 + 2O2 → H2O|The balanced equation has four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side.

Chemistry|In a closed system, what happens to total mass during an ordinary chemical reaction?|It remains constant|It always doubles|It always becomes zero|It depends only on the container's colour|Conservation of mass includes all reactants and products, including gases retained in the closed system.

Chemistry|A reaction releases heat to its surroundings. How is it described?|Exothermic|Endothermic|Always reversible|Always physical only|An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, often observed as heat release.

Chemistry|A reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings. How is it described?|Endothermic|Exothermic|Always explosive|Always neutralization|An endothermic reaction requires net energy input from the surroundings.

Chemistry|Which observation alone does NOT establish that a chemical reaction occurred?|A material is cut into smaller pieces|A new precipitate forms from solutions|A new gas evolves through reaction|A new substance with different properties forms|Changing size by cutting can leave chemical identity unchanged, whereas formation of new substances is evidence of reaction.

Chemistry|What is an element?|A substance whose atoms have the same proton number|Any material with two visible layers|A mixture of any two gases|Only a substance that dissolves in water|An element is identified by atomic number; it cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.

Chemistry|What is a compound?|A substance with different elements chemically combined in a fixed composition|Any combination separable by sieving|Every single atom|Only a liquid mixture|Compounds have a defined chemical composition and properties distinct from those of their constituent elements.

Chemistry|Which example is a mixture rather than a pure compound?|Air|Pure sodium chloride|Pure water|Pure carbon dioxide|Air contains several gases whose proportions can vary; its components are not one fixed chemical compound.

Chemistry|Which mixture is homogeneous at the scale of ordinary observation?|Salt fully dissolved in water|Sand mixed with stones|Oil layered on water|Soil containing visible pebbles|A dissolved salt solution has uniform composition throughout at ordinary scales, unlike the heterogeneous alternatives.

Chemistry|What is a solute in a solution?|The substance dissolved in the solvent|Always the container|Always a gas above the liquid|Only an insoluble residue|A solute is dissolved in a solvent; both can have different physical states depending on the solution.

Chemistry|What is a saturated solution at a specified temperature?|One containing the maximum amount of solute that can remain dissolved under those conditions|One containing no solute|One in which every possible substance dissolves|One that must be boiling|Saturation refers to an equilibrium solubility limit for a particular solute and solvent under stated conditions.

Chemistry|Why can ordinary filter paper not separate dissolved sugar from water?|Dissolved sugar passes through with the liquid|Sugar becomes an insoluble metal|The filter removes only water molecules|All dissolved substances evaporate instantly|Ordinary filtration retains sufficiently large insoluble particles; it does not remove molecularly dissolved sugar.

Chemistry|Which technique can recover solid salt from saltwater without collecting the water?|Evaporation|Magnetic separation|Sieving|Simple decantation of a uniform solution|Evaporating the solvent leaves nonvolatile salt behind; distillation would also collect condensed solvent.

Chemistry|Which method can separate iron filings from dry sand?|Magnetic separation|Neutralization|Condensation|Chromatography of light|A magnet attracts iron filings while ordinary sand is not strongly attracted.

Chemistry|Which technique can help separate the coloured components of an ink?|Paper chromatography|Sieving through a kitchen strainer|Magnetic separation|Melting the paper|Different dissolved components travel differently through the stationary phase with the mobile solvent.

Chemistry|Which change of state is sublimation?|Solid directly to gas|Gas to liquid|Liquid to solid|Solid to liquid|Sublimation bypasses the liquid state; the reverse gas-to-solid change is deposition.

Chemistry|What is condensation?|Gas changing to liquid|Solid changing directly to gas|Liquid changing to solid|Liquid changing to gas|Cooling a vapour under suitable conditions can cause it to form a liquid.

Chemistry|What is evaporation?|Liquid changing into vapour from its surface|Only solidification of a melt|Gas forming a solid directly|Formation of a new element|Evaporation occurs at a liquid's surface and need not wait until the liquid reaches its boiling point.

Chemistry|Which condition generally increases evaporation from water at the same temperature?|Greater exposed surface area|Smaller exposed surface area|Sealing the container completely|Reducing air movement while other factors stay equal|A larger surface gives more molecules an opportunity to escape; humidity and airflow also affect the rate.

Chemistry|How does blue litmus respond to a typical acidic aqueous solution?|It turns red|It turns green in every acid|It remains blue in every acid|It becomes a metal|Litmus is an acid-base indicator; acids turn blue litmus red under ordinary testing conditions.

Chemistry|How does red litmus respond to a typical basic aqueous solution?|It turns blue|It turns yellow in every base|It remains red in every base|It dissolves into oxygen|Bases turn red litmus blue under ordinary testing conditions.

Chemistry|What does a higher pH generally indicate when comparing ordinary aqueous solutions?|Lower hydrogen-ion activity|A larger atomic number|More neutrons in every atom|Greater mass regardless of volume|pH is related logarithmically to hydrogen-ion activity; increasing pH corresponds to decreasing activity.

Chemistry|Compared with pH 4, approximately how much greater is hydrogen-ion activity at pH 3?|Ten times|Twice|One half|One hundredth|A change of one pH unit represents a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion activity.

Chemistry|Which type of bonding involves sharing electron pairs between atoms?|Covalent bonding|Ionic bonding by definition only|Gravitational bonding|Mechanical fastening|Covalent bonds involve shared electron pairs, while ionic bonding is associated with electrostatic attraction between ions.

Chemistry|Which attraction primarily holds the ions together in sodium chloride?|Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions|Magnetic attraction between identical nuclei|Gravity alone|A string of neutral water molecules|Sodium and chloride ions form an ionic lattice maintained by electrostatic interactions.

Chemistry|Why can molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?|Its ions can move and carry charge|Its electrons become protons|All sodium atoms become magnets|Its neutrons carry electric current|Mobile ions carry current in the molten salt; ions in a solid lattice cannot move freely through it.

Chemistry|Which property is commonly associated with many metals?|Good electrical conductivity|Complete transparency in every case|Zero density|Inability to conduct any heat|Many metals have mobile electrons that support electrical and thermal conduction, although properties vary among metals.

Chemistry|What is an alloy?|A metallic material made by combining a metal with one or more other elements|Any pure noble gas|Only a dissolved sugar solution|A single isolated electron|Alloying can change strength, corrosion resistance and other properties; the added element need not itself be a metal.

Chemistry|What is galvanizing iron commonly intended to achieve?|Reduce corrosion using a protective zinc coating|Turn iron into a nonmetal|Remove all mass from iron|Make iron transparent|Zinc protects iron through a barrier and sacrificial corrosion behaviour when the coating is damaged.

Chemistry|Which statement about a catalyst in a reaction is correct?|It changes reaction rate without changing the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature|It always changes the element identities|It must be consumed as the final product|It makes conservation of atoms unnecessary|A catalyst changes the path and speeds approach to equilibrium; it does not change the thermodynamic equilibrium constant at a given temperature.

Chemistry|What distinguishes a reversible reaction in a closed chemical system?|Products can react to regenerate reactants|It can only happen once in the universe|It violates conservation of mass|It requires all materials to be solids|A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions; equilibrium involves equal forward and reverse rates, not necessarily equal amounts.

Biology|Which structure forms the selective boundary of a cell?|Cell membrane|Chromosome alone|Ribosome alone|Nucleolus alone|The cell membrane regulates exchange between the cell and its surroundings through several transport mechanisms.

Biology|Which structure is usually present in plant cells but absent from animal cells?|Cell wall|Cell membrane|Cytoplasm|Ribosomes|Plant cells usually have a cellulose-containing wall outside the membrane; both plant and animal cells have membranes and ribosomes.
Biology|Which organelle is responsible for protein synthesis?|Ribosome|Vacuole|Cell wall|Lysosome only|Ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins using information carried by messenger RNA.

Biology|What is diffusion?|Net movement from higher to lower concentration due to random particle motion|Movement requiring every particle to travel in one direction|Production of new atoms|Movement only of solid rocks|Random motion continues in both directions, but a concentration difference causes net movement down the gradient.

Biology|What is osmosis?|Net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane down its water-potential gradient|Movement only of proteins through air|Formation of new chromosomes|Movement of salt without any membrane|Osmosis concerns water movement across a selectively permeable membrane; solutes can influence the water-potential difference.

Biology|What is a tissue?|A group of cells organized to perform related functions|Any group of unrelated planets|Only one organ system|Every dissolved mineral|Tissues are organized cellular structures; several tissue types can contribute to one organ.

Biology|What is an organ system?|A set of organs working together in a major body function|A single electron|Only a colony of unrelated microbes|A cell's surrounding water only|For example, digestive organs work together to process food and absorb nutrients.

Biology|Where does gas exchange chiefly occur in the human lungs?|Alveoli|Tracheal cartilage|Vocal cords|Ribs|Alveoli provide thin exchange surfaces with nearby capillaries for diffusion of respiratory gases.

Biology|What is the basic role of the human heart?|Pump blood through the circulation|Produce all digestive enzymes|Store every chromosome|Filter urine directly|The heart generates pressure that moves blood through pulmonary and systemic circulations.

Biology|Which vessels carry blood away from the heart?|Arteries|Veins|Ureters|Bronchi|Vessel naming depends on direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content; pulmonary arteries carry relatively deoxygenated blood.
Biology|Which vessels carry blood toward the heart?|Veins|Arteries|Oesophagus|Trachea|Veins return blood to the heart; their oxygen content depends on the circuit.

Biology|Why are capillaries important in circulation?|Their thin walls support exchange with tissues|They replace every nerve|They make bones contract|They store all body oxygen permanently|Capillaries connect small arterial and venous vessels and provide surfaces for exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes.

Biology|What is the role of stomata in leaves?|Regulate gas exchange and water-vapour loss|Transport pollen through the root|Replace the plant's nucleus|Make soil minerals from sunlight|Stomatal pores controlled by guard cells influence carbon-dioxide entry and transpiration.

Biology|What is transpiration?|Loss of water vapour from aerial plant parts|Transfer of pollen to the stigma|Fusion of male and female gametes|Digestion of starch in the mouth|Water loss through stomata and other surfaces contributes to water movement and affects the plant's water balance.

Biology|What is the main role of root hairs?|Increase the surface for absorbing water and mineral ions|Produce pollen grains|Control every leaf's colour|Carry seeds between flowers|Root hairs are extensions of root epidermal cells that increase contact with soil solution.

Biology|What is a seed's embryo?|The developing young plant within the seed|Only the outer rock around the seed|A mature flower outside the seed|A fungal spore in every case|The embryo can develop into a new plant when germination conditions are suitable.

Biology|What does germination involve?|Resumption of embryo growth from a seed|Transfer of pollen between flowers only|Formation of a mineral vein|Conversion of all roots into leaves immediately|Germination commonly requires suitable water, oxygen and temperature; particular species may have additional requirements.

Biology|How does fertilization differ from pollination in flowering plants?|Fertilization is fusion of gametes; pollination is pollen transfer|Both mean only water uptake|Fertilization is soil drying|Pollination is always chromosome duplication|Pollen transfer enables subsequent processes that can lead to gamete fusion, but the terms describe distinct events.

Biology|Which example illustrates vegetative propagation?|A new plant growing from a potato tuber's bud|A bird laying an egg|Pollen moving in the wind only|A seed produced by fertilization only|Vegetative propagation produces new plants from nonseed plant structures such as tubers, stems or leaves.
Biology|Which molecule carries hereditary information in most organisms?|DNA|Starch|Cellulose|Water|DNA sequences encode hereditary information; some viruses have RNA genomes.

Biology|What is a gene in a basic genetics description?|A hereditary unit associated with a segment of DNA|Every visible organ as a whole|A dietary mineral|A type of blood vessel|Genes contribute to functional products and inherited characteristics, with expression influenced by biological context.

Biology|Why does sexual reproduction usually generate varied offspring?|It combines genetic information from parents and involves recombination and segregation|It always copies one parent without change|It removes all chromosomes|It prevents every mutation|The reshuffling and combination of genetic material contributes to variation among offspring.

Biology|What is an inherited trait?|A characteristic influenced by genetic information transmitted across generations|Every skill learned yesterday|Any temporary stain on clothing|Only a language spoken at school|Inherited traits reflect genetic transmission; acquired experiences are not automatically encoded as heritable DNA changes.

Biology|Which example is an acquired skill rather than a directly inherited trait?|Learning to ride a bicycle|An inherited blood-group characteristic|A genetically influenced seed colour|An inherited allele at a defined locus|A practised skill is learned through experience rather than being passed directly as that skill through genes.

Biology|What is natural selection?|Different survival and reproduction associated with heritable variation in a given environment|Organisms choosing every future mutation intentionally|Every individual becoming identical|The disappearance of all environmental effects|Heritable variants that contribute to reproductive success can become more frequent; populations change across generations.

Biology|What is a habitat?|The place and conditions in which an organism lives|Only its genetic code|Only the food in its stomach|Every continent regardless of occupancy|A habitat supplies environmental conditions and resources relevant to an organism's life.

Biology|What do decomposers contribute to an ecosystem?|Break down dead organic matter and help recycle nutrients|Create sunlight from soil|Stop all nutrient movement|Make every consumer photosynthetic|Fungi and many bacteria decompose organic material, returning nutrients to forms that other organisms can use.

Biology|Which relationship is predation?|One organism captures and consumes another|Two plants merely receiving sunlight|Water evaporating from a pond|A rock eroding in rain|Predation is a biological interaction in which a predator obtains food from prey.

Biology|What is a food web?|A network of interconnected feeding relationships|Only one organism's name|Only a map of roads|A list of rocks ordered by size|A food web shows multiple linked food chains and more realistically represents feeding pathways than a single chain.

Biology|Why does available energy generally decrease at successive trophic levels?|Energy is used in metabolism and much dissipates as heat rather than transferring to the next level|Energy is created anew without limit|Every organism passes all energy unchanged|Plants never absorb energy|Not all consumed material is assimilated, and organisms use energy for life processes; only a fraction becomes biomass available to the next level.

Biology|What is biodiversity?|Variation in living systems, including genes, species and ecosystems|Only the number of rocks in a forest|Only average rainfall|Only the height of the tallest tree|Biodiversity describes multiple levels of biological variation rather than one environmental measurement.

Biology|How can habitat fragmentation affect wildlife?|It can isolate populations and disrupt movement between suitable areas|It always increases every species' population|It removes all need for shelter|It makes every ecosystem identical|Breaking continuous habitats into smaller patches can alter resources, movement and genetic exchange, with effects varying by species.
